question: Fix a real point a and a natural number k, and prescribe target values v(0), v(1), ..., v(k). Define a degree-at-most-k real polynomial P by taking the local Taylor polynomial centred at a whose coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j!. Prove that for every j with 0 <= j <= k the ordinary j-th derivative of P evaluated at a equals exactly v(j). You may use the fact that the j-th derivative of a polynomial at a point equals j! times the degree-j Taylor coefficient of the polynomial about that point.
reference_answer: Write P = sum over i in {0,...,k} of (v(i)/i!) * (x-a)^i. The key bridge is that for any polynomial Q, (d^j/dx^j Q)(a) = j! * c_j, where c_j is the coefficient of (x-a)^j in the Taylor expansion of Q about a; equivalently c_j is the degree-j coefficient of the shifted polynomial Q(x+a). Step 1: the Taylor coefficients of P about a are read off directly: the coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j! for j <= k and 0 for j > k, because P is already written in the (x-a) basis. Step 2: apply the bridge at order j <= k: (d^j P/dx^j)(a) = j! * (coefficient of (x-a)^j) = j! * (v(j)/j!). Step 3: since j! is a nonzero natural number cast into the reals, j! * (v(j)/j!) = v(j) exactly. Hence every requested jet value is reproduced, and the construction has degree at most k, has degree at most k. The bound k is the generic (worst-case) degree needed to carry k+1 derivative constraints at a single node; particular data may be realised by a lower-degree polynomial (all-zero data gives the zero polynomial, and if v(k)=0 the degree drops below k), so k is an upper bound on this construction's degree, not a universal minimum for every data vector. No approximation is involved: the identities are exact real-polynomial identities.

question: Fix the clean signal value. Prove that the following two certificate conditions are equivalent: (i) the projected system x system block of U equals a target A entrywise; (ii) for every system basis input and output, the clean output amplitude of U on the clean basis input (clean signal, basis input) equals A(output,input). Explain each direction, name the single linear-algebra fact that makes one clean-basis amplitude equal to one projected-block entry, and state how (ii) extends from basis inputs to an arbitrary normalized system input.
reference_answer: Write the compound (flattened) index for signal value s and system index k as s*systemDim + k, with s fixed to the clean value throughout. The projected block entry at (output,input) is block(output,input) = U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input). The clean output amplitude is the coordinate at compound index (clean,output) of the vector U applied to the basis ket at compound index (clean,input). Key fact: applying a matrix to a computational basis ket selects the corresponding column of the matrix (mulVec of a single-one indicator yields that column). Hence the clean output amplitude equals U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input), which is exactly block(output,input). (i) => (ii): if block = A entrywise, then for each (output,input) the clean output amplitude equals block(output,input) = A(output,input). (ii) => (i): if every clean output amplitude equals A(output,input), then by the same column-selection identity every projected-block entry equals A(output,input), so block = A entrywise. The two statements are therefore pointwise equivalent at the fixed signal value. Extension to arbitrary input: write a normalized system state as a linear combination of system basis vectors; the clean output on this input is the same linear combination of the per-basis clean outputs by linearity of matrix-vector action, so the clean-branch action equals A acting on the system state (up to the normalizer and the orthogonal failure branch, which only records the unitarity probability deficit). This equivalence is why a construction may prove the block directly or prove the clean action and conclude the other.

question: A block encoding is read by preparing the auxiliary register in the all-zero state, applying U, and postselecting the auxiliary register back on all-zero. Suppose U block-encodes A with normalizer alpha (so the auxiliary-zero projected block equals A/alpha) and the input system state is a normalized vector v. Express the unnormalized clean output branch and its squared norm, give the exact success probability of the all-zero postselection, and state when this probability equals (||A v|| / alpha)^2. Why is the success probability generally strictly below 1, and what does this cost imply for using the block encoding as a subroutine?
reference_answer: Prepare |0^a> tensor |v>, apply U. Decompose the output as |0^a> tensor w_clean + (orthogonal auxiliary-nonzero branches), where w_clean = (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor |v>). Because the auxiliary-zero projected block of U equals A/alpha, w_clean = (A/alpha) v. The all-zero postselection keeps exactly the clean branch, so the unnormalized clean output is (A/alpha) v with squared norm ||(A/alpha) v||^2 = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2, and the post-measurement normalized state is (A v)/||A v||. The success probability of the all-zero auxiliary outcome is therefore p = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2 = (||A v|| / alpha)^2. This equals (||A v||/alpha)^2 exactly whenever the projected block is exactly A/alpha (the exact block-encoding case); in the epsilon-approximate case it is this value up to an O(epsilon) correction. Since U is unitary, the total output norm is 1, so p <= 1 with equality only in the degenerate case ||A v|| = alpha (e.g. alpha = ||A|| and v a top singular vector with the orthogonal branch empty); generically ||A v|| < alpha (alpha is chosen at least the operator norm so the encoding is valid for all v), so p < 1 strictly. The cost implication: one query to U succeeds with probability p that can be far below 1, so naive repetition costs O(1/p) = O(alpha^2/||A v||^2) trials; amplitude amplification reduces this to O(alpha/||A v||) queries. This 1/alpha success penalty is exactly why the normalizer alpha is a charged resource and why alpha should be kept close to ||A||.

question: An exact clean-block certificate can be promoted to a zero-error approximate incumbent in the adaptive exact-to-approximate search policy. State what data an exact clean-block certificate carries, what the zero-error promotion sets the epsilon and the approximation predicate to, and why an exact certificate is a legitimate epsilon=0 member of the approximate search without any additional analytic norm argument. Then explain the boundary the other way: does holding a zero-error approximate incumbent let you conclude an operator-norm bound ||A - alpha*block|| <= 0, and if not, what extra ingredient is required?
reference_answer: An exact clean-block certificate carries: a full matrix U on the total (ancilla+system) basis, a target system-space matrix A, an embedding of the system basis into the total basis, and a proof that the embedded clean block of U equals A pointwise (the clean submatrix equals A entry by entry). The zero-error promotion sets epsilon = 0 and sets the approximation predicate to be exactly that same pointwise clean-block equality, with the approximation proof being the certificate's own block proof. This is legitimate because the approximate incumbent's bound field is a PROPOSITION that different backends may instantiate; the exact finite route instantiates the epsilon=0 bound by the exact pointwise equality it already proved, so no analytic operator-norm reasoning is introduced - the promotion is a repackaging, not a new theorem. Boundary the other way: holding this zero-error approximate incumbent does NOT by itself yield the analytic statement ||A - alpha*block|| <= 0 in an operator-norm sense. The finite certificate proves ENTRYWISE (pointwise) equality of the clean block with A/normalizer; converting that to an operator-norm inequality (or to the statement that the operator-norm distance is 0) requires the extra ingredient of a theorem connecting pointwise/entrywise equality of finite matrices to the chosen matrix norm (e.g. that pointwise equality implies equality as operators and hence zero norm difference). The source is explicit that analytic backends can LATER replace the exact-as-approximate packaging with such a theorem; until then the epsilon=0 incumbent is a faithful exact-equality witness, not an analytic norm certificate. So the exact-to-approximate direction is free (repackaging), but the approximate-norm interpretation needs an added norm-vs-pointwise bridge.

question: Suppose a non-unitary matrix A acting on n qubits is embedded as the top-left block of a larger unitary, in the sense that applying the unitary to an input with the ancilla register prepared in all-zeros, and then measuring the ancillas and keeping only the all-zeros outcome, applies A to the system state. More generally the embedded block equals A divided by a positive subnormalization factor alpha. For an input system state |b>, derive the probability of the kept (all-zeros) outcome, express it in terms of A, |b> and alpha, and explain two consequences: how the norm of A|b> can be recovered from the measured success probability, and why choosing alpha too large is harmful. Confirm the output state conditioned on success is the correctly normalized version of A|b>.
reference_answer: Apply the unitary to |0...0>|b>. By the block structure the component in the all-zeros ancilla sector is |0...0> (A/alpha)|b>, and the rest is orthogonal to the all-zeros ancilla subspace. The probability of measuring the ancillas in all-zeros is the squared norm of that component: p(0) = ||(A/alpha)|b>||^2 = (1/alpha^2) <b| A-dagger A |b> = ||A|b>||^2 / alpha^2. In the exact one-ancilla case alpha = 1 this is simply p(0) = ||A|b>||^2 = <b|A-dagger A|b>. Consequence 1 (norm recovery): the norm that is 'lost' when the output is renormalized is encoded in the success probability, since ||A|b>|| = alpha sqrt(p(0)); measuring p(0) (by repetition) therefore recovers ||A|b>||. Consequence 2 (cost of large alpha): p(0) scales as 1/alpha^2, so an unnecessarily large alpha makes the all-zeros outcome exponentially unlikely and the scheme requires on the order of alpha^2/||A|b>||^2 repetitions (or amplitude amplification) to succeed, which is why one wants the smallest valid alpha (at least the operator norm of A). Output state on success: dividing the kept component by its own norm gives (A/alpha)|b> / ||(A/alpha)|b>|| = A|b> / ||A|b>||, the correctly normalized image of |b> under A, independent of alpha and of the irrelevant orthogonal part of the unitary.

question: When a matrix A is embedded (up to a positive factor alpha) as the all-zeros block of a larger unitary, so that A/alpha is a submatrix of a unitary, prove the necessary scaling constraint on alpha. First prove the auxiliary fact that any submatrix block of a unitary has operator norm at most 1. Deduce the sharp lower bound alpha must satisfy in terms of the operator norm of A, explain why an exact unit-factor embedding is impossible when A has operator norm bigger than 1, and state what role alpha then plays and whether the bound alone guarantees an efficiently implementable embedding.
reference_answer: Submatrix-norm fact: let U be unitary and let B = P U Q be a block, where P and Q are projectors onto the output and input index sets of the block (equivalently B = <0^m| U |0^m> as an operator on the system register). For any unit input vector v (extended by zeros outside the block), ||B v|| = ||P U (Q v)|| <= ||U (Q v)|| = ||Q v|| <= ||v|| = 1, since projectors are norm-nonincreasing and U is norm-preserving. Taking the supremum over unit v gives ||B|| <= 1. Lower bound on alpha: if A/alpha is such a block of a unitary, then ||A/alpha|| <= 1, i.e. ||A|| <= alpha, so alpha >= ||A|| is necessary. In particular if ||A|| > 1 there is no exact embedding with alpha = 1 (a unit-factor block would force ||A|| <= 1); one must take alpha >= ||A|| > 1. Role of alpha: it rescales A so that A/alpha fits inside a unitary as a contraction, at the cost of a success probability that falls like 1/alpha^2; the smallest admissible alpha is the operator norm ||A|| (achieved by a singular-value dilation). Finally, the inequality alpha >= ||A|| is only a necessary existence condition on the scale: it does not by itself provide a circuit, since constructing a unitary whose block is A/alpha and that is implementable with few elementary gates requires further structure or oracle access to A; the bound guarantees feasibility of the scale, not efficiency of implementation.

question: A target operator is written as a linear combination T = sum_i alpha_i U_i of unitaries U_i, and is implemented by a prepare-select-unprepare scheme in which each coefficient is split as alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, a left preparation loads the vector of beta_i (normalized by the 2-norm of beta), a controlled selection applies U_i, and a right unpreparation loads the vector of gamma_i. The resulting construction embeds T with subnormalization factor equal to the product of the 2-norms of the beta and gamma vectors. Prove, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, that this subnormalization factor is at least the 1-norm of the coefficient vector alpha, and determine the splitting beta_i, gamma_i that makes the factor equal to that 1-norm. Explain why this is the best (smallest) achievable factor for this scheme and hence the most favorable success probability.
reference_answer: The scheme produces subnormalization factor ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 where ||beta||_2 = sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) and likewise for gamma. Since alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, the 1-norm of alpha is ||alpha||_1 = sum_i |alpha_i| = sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i|. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the vectors (|beta_i|)_i and (|gamma_i|)_i, sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i| <= sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) sqrt(sum_i |gamma_i|^2) = ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2. Therefore ||alpha||_1 <= ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2, i.e. the subnormalization factor is at least ||alpha||_1 for every admissible split. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds iff the vectors (|beta_i|) and (|gamma_i|) are proportional; combined with |beta_i gamma_i| = |alpha_i|, the symmetric optimum is |beta_i| = |gamma_i| = sqrt(|alpha_i|) for every i. With that choice ||beta||_2^2 = ||gamma||_2^2 = sum_i |alpha_i| = ||alpha||_1, so ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 = ||alpha||_1, attaining the lower bound. Since the success probability of keeping the all-zeros ancilla scales inversely with the square of the subnormalization factor, minimizing it to ||alpha||_1 maximizes the success probability for this prepare-select-unprepare implementation; no split in this scheme can do better, because ||alpha||_1 is a hard lower bound from Cauchy-Schwarz. (When all alpha_i >= 0 this optimal choice also makes the unpreparation the adjoint of the preparation.)

question: Consider the exact right-canonicalization of a finite real tensor train. Characterize the active (reduced) bond dimensions it produces: give the backward recurrence the reduced left rank of each core obeys, prove the two-sided bound on the head rank of any nonempty canonicalized train, and derive the sharp consequence that the penultimate active bond of a scalar-to-scalar train (one core, both boundaries dimension one) has dimension at most two. Also state why canonicalization never enlarges the maximal bond.
reference_answer: Right-canonicalization reduces each core by a thin factorization whose Q-factor row count is min(l, 2*m'), where l is the current left dimension and m' is the already-reduced next bond. So the reduced left rank obeys the backward min recurrence l' = min(l, 2*m') computed from the terminal bond inward. Two-sided head bound: for any nonempty canonicalized train D = cons Q tail with reduced head l', from l' = min(l, 2*m') we get both l' <= l (the min is at most its first argument) and l' <= 2*m' (the min is at most its second argument), where m' is the next active bond. Thus the head rank is bounded by the original left dimension and by twice the next active rank simultaneously. Sharp scalar case: for a one-core chain with both boundaries dimension one (Chain 1 l 1), the tail is the empty chain whose only bond is the terminal bond of dimension one, so m' = 1. The head bound l' <= 2*m' becomes l' <= 2. This is sharp: a core emitting one bit from a scalar boundary can legitimately populate both values of that bit, so the reduced bond genuinely reaches dimension two. No enlargement: the maximal bond of D is bounded by that of the original chain, because each reduced left rank min(l, 2*m') is at most l and, inductively, the tail's maximal bond does not grow; taking the max over cores preserves the inequality. Hence canonicalization is a non-expanding rank reduction with an explicit min recurrence and a tight penultimate-bond-at-most-two corollary.

native_nl.core_summary: Zero sibling pairs are harmless vanishing subtrees handled by angle zero; only a globally zero vector breaks the normalized first-column identity, so strict positivity of the total norm is the minimal honest hypothesis.

question: The recursive real-amplitude loader assigns the all-zero sibling pair the angle zero, so a vanishing subtree contributes no rotation. (i) Explain operationally what a zero sibling pair means for the prepared state and why angle zero is the right choice there. (ii) The sharp first-column theorem that recovers f(b)/sqrt(normSq f) for every entry is stated with a STRICT positivity hypothesis on the entries, yet the construction clearly tolerates many exact zeros internally. Reconcile these: identify where exact interior zeros are harmless and where a zero would actually break the stated per-entry identity, and give the minimal honest hypothesis for the whole-vector claim.
reference_answer: (i) A zero sibling pair (a = b = 0) means the entire subtree hanging below that split carries no amplitude: the marginal mass at that prefix is zero, so there is nothing to rotate between the two children. The rotation angle multiplies a zero marginal in the first-column recursion, so any angle would give the same (zero) contribution; assigning angle zero is the canonical, well-defined choice and avoids an undefined polar angle (a/0). The split-level identity still holds exactly at a zero pair because both children are forced to zero and the rotation applied to a zero norm yields zero. So interior zeros that occur as whole vanishing subtrees are harmless: the marginal recursion and the per-split identity both pass through them. (ii) The strict positivity hypothesis in the sharp flat theorem is NOT needed for the circuit to be unitary or for the general first-column recursion, which only needs the global norm to be positive (so sqrt(normSq f) is nonzero and the normalized target f(b)/sqrt(normSq f) is well defined). Where a zero genuinely bites is subtler: if the TOTAL norm is zero (all entries zero) the normalization sqrt(normSq f) = 0 and f(b)/sqrt(normSq f) is 0/0, so the per-entry identity is vacuous/ill-posed; strict positivity of the total norm is the real load-bearing condition. The entrywise strict positivity in the convenience API is a sufficient simplification (it guarantees positive total norm and lets the proof avoid case-splitting on vanishing subtrees), but it is stronger than necessary: the honest minimal hypothesis for the whole-vector normalized first-column claim is that the total squared norm is strictly positive (equivalently, at least one entry is nonzero), with individual entries allowed to be zero or negative. Thus zeros inside the tree are fine; only a globally zero vector breaks the stated identity.
